strengths: Well-motivated problem: clinical need for CT reconstruction models that generalize across sampling rates and resolutions without retraining is clearly articulated and practically relevant.

Solid architectural design combining sinogram-space and image-space neural operators within an unrolled network, with a rotation-equivariant sinogram operator justified both theoretically (Appendix A) and via ablation.

Strong and consistent empirical gains over CNN, transformer (DuDoTrans, GloReDi), and diffusion (DPS, ALD) baselines across two datasets (Kidney CT, AAPM Abdomen) and multiple sparse-view settings (9/18/36/72 views), with clear PSNR/SSIM/RMSE improvements.
Practical advantage of ~500x faster inference than diffusion-based competitors while achieving better reconstruction quality, which is compelling for deployment.
Useful ablations isolating the contribution of rotational equivariance and of different frequency-domain learning configurations in the sinogram operator, supporting the design choices.

Zero-shot super-resolution experiments (both image-space and sinogram-space) demonstrate genuine resolution-agnostic behavior beyond the trained configurations, which is a meaningful validation of the core claim.
weaknesses: The core building blocks (DISCO convolutions, UDNO block) are adopted directly from prior work (Ocampo et al., Jatyani et al.), so the technical novelty largely lies in the CT-specific sinogram-domain formulation and rotation-equivariant padding scheme rather than a fundamentally new operator design; this should be more explicitly contextualized relative to the closely related MRI unified-model paper [22].

The 'resolution-agnostic across image resolutions' claim is validated mainly via zero-shot super-resolution rather than joint training across multiple output resolutions (unlike the sampling-rate experiments, which do use joint multi-rate training), making the cross-resolution generalization claim slightly weaker than the cross-sampling-rate claim.

Only two datasets are evaluated, both abdominal/kidney CT with similar geometry; broader validation (e.g., other anatomies, real clinical noise/artifact conditions, metal artifacts, limited-angle CT) would strengthen claims of general applicability.

The rotational-equivariance ablation shows a relatively modest improvement (0.83 dB), and it is unclear how much of the overall performance gain versus CNN baselines stems from this component versus the broader operator/dual-domain architecture.
No public code or data release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the architectural complexity (multiple UDNO branches, custom padding schemes, kernel basis hyperparameters).

Comparisons to other neural operator baselines (e.g., FNO-based CT models) are absent; only CNN, transformer, and diffusion baselines are considered, leaving open whether the specific DISCO/local-kernel choice is superior to alternative NO architectures for this task.
3D CT extension, which is clinically more relevant than 2D slices, is left as future work, somewhat limiting immediate real-world impact.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clinically relevant limitation of existing CT reconstruction networks — their inability to generalize across sampling rates and resolutions without retraining separate models — and is (to the authors' claim) the first application of neural operators to sparse-view CT.

Thorough empirical evaluation across two/three datasets (AAPM, Kidney/C4KC-KiTS, LIDC-IDRI in supplement), multiple sampling rates (9/18/36/72-view), and a wide range of baselines spanning learning-free, diffusion, single-pass, and unrolled-network categories.

Well-motivated architectural design: sinogram-domain operator in polar coordinates with joint spatial-frequency (Fourier-slice-theorem-inspired) processing, and rotation-equivariant circular padding with a formal derivation of the symmetry (Supp. A).

Strong and consistent empirical gains: >3.4dB PSNR over CNN baseline, ~3dB over diffusion SOTA with >500x faster inference, and clear zero-shot super-resolution benefits in both image and sinogram domains.

Extensive ablations (NOs/NOi component removal, rotational equivariance, frequency-transform axis choice, DISCO kernel hyperparameter sensitivity via Bayesian search, single-rate vs multi-rate training, OOD/noisy/cross-dataset generalization) that support the design choices and improve confidence in the results.
Careful complexity/runtime analysis showing DISCO-based operators match CNN inference cost while incurring only modest training-time overhead, addressing practical deployability concerns.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: DISCO convolutions and the U-shaped DISCO block are adopted largely unchanged from prior work (Liu-Schiaffini et al., Jatyani et al. for MRI); the main contribution is applying/adapting these established building blocks to a new domain (CT) with a dual-domain, polar-coordinate arrangement, rather than introducing a fundamentally new operator or theory.

All experiments use simulated sinograms generated from existing CT images via a forward Radon/fan-beam operator rather than real raw clinical acquisition data, which may not fully capture real scanner noise characteristics, detector nonlinearities, or other practical acquisition artifacts.
Only 2D reconstruction is studied; 3D CT (clinically standard for many protocols) is left to future work, limiting immediate clinical applicability despite motivating claims about clinical practice.

Baseline retraining under the multi-rate protocol departs from baselines' original single-rate designs, and some baseline numbers (e.g., DuDoTrans SSIM) appear much lower than in their original papers; while the authors flag this, it raises some concern about whether all baselines were optimally tuned for the multi-rate setting, potentially inflating the apparent margin of improvement.

The rotation-equivariance property is formally established only for the sinogram-space operator; it is not clearly shown (theoretically or empirically beyond qualitative visualization) that this equivariance is preserved through the image-space operator and data-consistency steps to yield exact end-to-end equivariance.

Zero-shot super-resolution across image resolutions relies on a bilinear upsampling step between the fixed-resolution sinogram operator and the higher-resolution image operator, which is a partly ad hoc bridge rather than a fully native cross-resolution operator design.
Limited discussion of failure modes, error bars/statistical significance testing between CTO and closest baselines, or qualitative analysis of when/why CTO underperforms, if at all.
